At the edge of every city there is a place where certainty begins to thin.

Streetlights become sparse. Buildings give way to warehouses, then empty lots, then fields that look almost black at night. The roads widen strangely, as if expecting more traffic than they receive. Signs point toward towns with names you have never heard spoken aloud.

It is easy to think of these places as unfinished. But perhaps they are not unfinished at all. Perhaps they are pauses.

A pause is not emptiness. It is a room in which something can be heard.

In the pause between thunder and rain, the trees hold still. In the pause before someone answers a difficult question, entire histories pass across their face. In the pause after a train leaves, the platform seems to remember everyone who stood there.

We fill our lives with small machines designed to erase pauses: screens, music, notifications, schedules, bright advertisements in elevators. Silence can feel accusatory. It asks us to meet ourselves without witnesses.

But sometimes, late at night, the power goes out.

The refrigerator stops humming. The little lights on chargers vanish. The house becomes larger and older. You hear the wind testing the windows. You hear pipes cooling in the walls. You hear your own breathing, unexpectedly present.

For a few minutes, perhaps, you are returned to a more ancient world: one with darkness, weather, distance, and the remarkable fact that you are here at all.

Then the power comes back. The appliances resume their work. The clocks blink incorrect numbers. Somewhere, a neighbor cheers or curses.

And the world continues—not because the silence was defeated, but because it was allowed to exist for a while.
